question_technical: Is there excess mass just below the threshold that triggers competitive tender?
title_technical: Are tenders bunched just under the public-tender limit?
objection: A clean bunching test only catches the crudest form of threshold gaming — splitting one job into two separately tendered pieces, or timing a contract just outside the amount-based rule, would not show up as a pile-up in this dollar histogram at all.
response: That is the honest limit of a distributional test: it can only see gaming that leaves a visible fingerprint in the amount distribution itself. What it does rule out is the simplest and most common form — deliberately shaving a contract's value down to duck the competitive-tender threshold — which is exactly the pattern real procurement-integrity audits look for first.

question_technical: Is any supplier both a frequent repeat-winner and a big-dollar incumbent?
title_technical: Do the same firms keep winning the big contracts?
objection: Looking only for a firm that is both a frequent repeat-winner and a top-dollar recipient could miss quieter forms of favouritism — a firm that wins consistently without ever cracking the top-dollar list, or one that captures the dollars without winning many separate awards.
response: The two-part overlap test is deliberately a high bar, aimed at the clearest capture signature: an entrenched supplier a council keeps handing both frequent and lucrative work. A quieter pattern would need a different measure, but this one catches the single most recognisable form of supplier-panel risk auditors flag first.

question_technical: What share of tenders had no competitive field?
title_technical: Single-source / direct-negotiation share
objection: Without a recorded count of how many firms bid on each tender, there is no way to see how much work goes to a single bidder with no real competition — a genuine gap in what this corpus can show, not a clean bill of health.
response: This is carried in the battery specifically so that gap stays visible and comparable: a council whose minutes do record competitive-field size will produce a real result here, and this council's blank result is itself a flagged re-extraction target, not a silently skipped test.

question_technical: Is tendered spend concentrated, and how much is awarded confidentially?
title_technical: Where did the tender money go?
objection: A handful of firms capturing most of the named contract dollars is exactly what capture would look like — concentration this heavy doesn't, on its own, rule out favouritism toward a small circle of suppliers.
response: Concentration among a handful of large contractors is the ordinary shape of big civil-works spending, not evidence of capture by itself — what would distinguish the two is corroborating evidence, and here there is none: independent tests for threshold-gaming, entrenched incumbency and repeat-player advantage on this same tender record all come back clean. The share of spend that goes to a confidential, unnamed recipient is a genuine transparency gap worth watching in its own right, separate from the concentration question.

question_technical: When council awards a tender, is a conflict declared — and does the winner ever match a councillor's known connections?
title_technical: Do tender deciders share an undeclared connection with the winner?
objection: Only tender-award votes that were separately moved and recorded show up here — an award nodded through as part of a bundled consent agenda, with no individual vote to check, is invisible to this join entirely.
response: That coverage gap is real, and the result should be read within it. What the test does establish, across every tender-award vote it can see, is that the two checkable signatures of a hidden connection — a shared surname with a councillor, or an interest that should have been declared but wasn't — turn up nothing, consistent with the separate clean results for threshold-gaming and incumbency on the supplier side.

question_technical: When an interest is declared, is it *managed* — i.e. does the member recuse?
title_technical: Do councillors step out when they declare a conflict?
objection: Declaring a conflict looks like disclosure theatre if the councillor who declares it goes on to vote anyway — a safeguard that only requires saying the words changes nothing in practice.
response: Disclosure is real, not cosmetic: declaring an interest measurably raises the chance a member steps out, and many of these declarations are lawful 'impartiality' interests the member is entitled to stay and vote on regardless. But that only clears the identify-and-disclose half of the safeguard — the *manage* half still breaks more often than it holds, since staying in the room and voting is still the more common outcome once an interest is declared.

question_technical: Did stepping out of serious conflicts change around external scrutiny?
title_technical: Did recusal compliance track the Authorised Inquiry?
objection: The apparent fall in recusal is just an artefact of composition — declarations shifted toward lawful 'impartiality' interests where the member is entitled to stay, so nothing about actual mandatory-conflict behaviour changed.
response: Impartiality declarations did increase substantially, so part of the composition shift is real. But the decline shows up *within* the must-leave categories too, not only in the mix between them — proximity-conflict recusal fell after the period of heightened external scrutiny, not just its share of all declarations. Financial conflicts are too rare on their own to show a trend either way, so the within-category evidence rests on the proximity category, not the financial one.

question_technical: When a councillor is Council's own appointed delegate/board member on an external body, do they declare an interest before voting on that body's business — the same disclosure regime a private supplier relationship gets?
title_technical: Do council-appointed delegates declare on their own body's business?
objection: The sample behind this is thin — one body's affiliated-vote count barely clears double digits — so a single mis-attributed vote could shift an individual body's rate noticeably.
response: The small per-body counts are why no single body's raw percentage is treated as the finding — what the test reads instead is the *contrast* between bodies: seats that are a public appointment, not a personal stake, cluster near zero, while the one body where councillors can hold a genuine private interest sits materially higher. That shape is a more robust signal than any one body's number, even at this sample size.

question_technical: Does approval rate vary with the estimated value of the development?
title_technical: Do big-dollar developments get an easier ride?
objection: Splitting applications into four value quartiles can only catch a leniency effect that's smooth across the whole value range — a council that goes easy on one specific tier of big-money projects, without shifting the other quartiles, could still show up as a flat overall spread.
response: A coarse quartile split is a deliberately blunt first pass: it's the measure that would catch the most legible form of value-based leniency, a steady tilt from cheap to expensive projects. It doesn't rule out a narrower pattern, but establishing that the broad relationship is flat is still worth knowing before looking for something subtler.

question_technical: Do repeat builders/agents get approved at a higher rate than one-shot applicants?
title_technical: Do frequent applicants win approval more often?
objection: Bucketing by how many applications a name has filed can miss a repeat-applicant advantage that runs through an agent or a company structure rather than an individual's own name, or one that only shows up for a handful of the most prolific filers.
response: Grouping by named applicant is the most direct read of favouritism the record supports, and it's a deliberately generous test for a real effect: if repeat filers were getting an easier ride, the highest-frequency bucket is exactly where it would show up first. A flat result across frequency bands rules out the most legible form of that risk, even if it can't see one hidden behind a shifting company name.

question_technical: Does refusal rise with the number of residents objecting to an application?
title_technical: Does the council respond to community objection?
objection: A dose-response curve built on objector count assumes numbers are what matters — it wouldn't catch a council that ignores volume but responds instead to who is objecting, or to organised opposition that never shows up as many individual submissions.
response: Objector count is the most basic, most checkable form of 'does volume of opposition change the outcome', and it's the one a dose-response test is built to answer cleanly. That the refusal rate climbs with objector count rules out the most common complaint about planning processes — that objecting is pointless — even if it can't speak to influence that runs through channels other than counted submissions.

question_technical: How often does council depart from the officer recommendation?
title_technical: Does the chamber decide, or ratify its officers?
objection: If officers get their way almost every time, 'debate' is theatre and the substantive decision is really made upstream, in whoever writes the recommendation — the council vote is a formality.
response: Exceptions are a genuine minority, not an absent check: every recorded departure from an officer recommendation is listed and inspectable here, not buried inside an otherwise-unanimous-looking vote. Divergence is rare, but it is real, and it is auditable rather than assumed.

question_technical: On contested votes, how unequal is who actually wins — and is it accountable?
title_technical: Does consensus hide a power hierarchy?
objection: However contested a vote looks on paper, the same handful of councillors win most of the time, so 'debate' is theatre for a fixed majority — some members are consistently on the losing side more often than the winning one.
response: That spread resets every election rather than calcifying around one clique — the term-by-term picture shows real churn in who ends up on top. And dissent is not merely symbolic: a meaningful share of contested motions actually fail, so objecting carries real leverage, not just recorded protest.

question_technical: Does membership on the council's Audit Committee / CEO Performance Review Committee skew toward the chamber's habitual winners, or draw broadly — including from its habitual dissenters?
title_technical: Is the council's own oversight function captured by its most powerful members?
objection: Pooling decades into one win-rate comparison could hide a modern-era shift — an oversight body that has become more or less representative recently would not necessarily move the all-time average, and the appointee win-rate methodology here isn't directly comparable to the chamber-wide power test elsewhere in this battery.
response: The era-pooled comparison is the most data the appointee cohort can support, and even at that scale the point holds: appointee win rates run across almost the whole spectrum of the chamber, from consistent winners to frequent dissenters, rather than clustering among the powerful. A modern-era-only cut is a natural refinement, not a reason to doubt the pooled result.

question_technical: What share of carried motions drew at least one dissenting vote, over time?
title_technical: How often does the chamber actually split?
principles: CIPFA-B — how the chamber conducts business
objection: Counting only carried motions that drew a recorded dissenting vote misses everything that gets negotiated, watered down, or quietly withdrawn before it ever reaches a vote — a chamber could look mostly unanimous simply because disagreement gets resolved off the record, not because it doesn't exist.
response: That is a real limit of any vote-based contestation measure, and it's worth stating plainly rather than reading a high unanimity rate as proof of either a rubber-stamp chamber or a harmonious one. What the trend does show reliably is how the *recorded* contested share moves over time, which is exactly the kind of era-to-era comparison this measure is built for.

question_technical: Do the Mayor's own motions get an easier ride than backbench motions?
title_technical: Does the council fall in line behind the Mayor?
objection: A high dissent rate on the Mayor's own motions doesn't rule out influence exercised off the floor — a mayor could still shape which items reach a vote at all, or how they're framed beforehand, in ways the recorded vote never sees. And only mayors with a dated term are compared this way at all; earlier mayoralties fall into the general backbench count.
response: Those are real limits of a vote-count measure, but they cut against the more common failure mode, not around it: the usual sign of chair capture is a chamber that waves the chair's motions through with unusually little dissent. Here the opposite happens — a chamber that votes against its own Mayor more than it does against the backbench is direct evidence against that specific risk, even without being able to see influence exercised before a vote is called.

question_technical: Do voting/sponsorship blocs persist across electoral terms (an entrenched bloc)?
title_technical: Is there a faction that survives across elections?
caveats: Descriptive structural history, not a significance test: cross-term persistence rests on too few high-lift sponsorship edges per electoral term to prove statistically.
objection: A sponsorship network that looks dense and long-lived could just be pattern-matching on a small, noisy sample — with only a handful of high-lift ties surviving each electoral term, what looks like a persistent faction could be coincidence dressed up as a network.
response: This is descriptive structural history, not a significance test: the consolidation and later fragmentation is a real, visible pattern in who sponsored whom, but cross-term persistence rests on too few high-lift edges per term to prove statistically. Read the shape — a bloc that formed, held for years, then broke apart with no comparable successor — as the finding, not any single edge's exact weight.

question_technical: How entrenched is the chamber — long-server-heavy, or renewing?
title_technical: Career councillors vs one-term members
objection: Measuring tenure by the span of a councillor's recorded votes will understate anyone whose early records are thin or who cast too few votes to clear the activity floor this test uses — a long-serving but quiet member could be invisible to this measure entirely.
response: That undercount runs in one direction only — toward understating entrenchment, never manufacturing it — so a long-server-heavy tail found this way is, if anything, a floor on the real figure. The measure is still the most direct read the record supports of how much institutional memory concentrates in a few hands versus turning over.

question_technical: Do councillors dissent at a different rate in their first year than later?
title_technical: Are new councillors bolder or tamer than veterans?
objection: A simple early-vs-late split is confounded by which era a councillor's first year happens to fall in — since freshmen cluster in whichever years saw the most turnover, a pooled comparison can pick up the era's mood rather than anything about being new.
response: That confound is exactly why the pooled early-vs-late figures here are read as descriptive, not causal — and the more rigorous per-councillor comparison that controls for era came back a clean null. Reporting both the naive comparison and that caveat, rather than only the flattering one, is the point of running the test at all.

question_technical: Is dissent higher in the pre-election window than the rest of the cycle?
title_technical: Do councillors grandstand before elections?
objection: A single, jurisdiction-wide election window is a blunt instrument — it can't separate a councillor genuinely grandstanding ahead of their own re-election from ordinary year-to-year variation in how contested the agenda happens to be.
response: It's a deliberately simple test for a specific, checkable claim — that dissent spikes in the run-up to an election — and a small, confound-prone difference is itself the honest answer: it doesn't support a strong electoral-positioning effect, rather than manufacturing one out of a blunt window.

question_technical: What share of cast-vote opportunities are ABSENT, and is that recusal or disengagement?
title_technical: How often are councillors absent — and is it recusal or non-attendance?
objection: Splitting ABSENT votes into lawful recusal and genuine non-attendance depends on a declared interest being recorded on that specific motion — a councillor who was simply away with no conflict declared and no recorded reason is counted correctly, but an undeclared conflict would be misclassified as ordinary non-attendance rather than a recusal that should have been declared.
response: That risk sits with the conflict-declaration tests elsewhere in this battery, not this one — here, taking the record at face value, the ABSENT figure is overwhelmingly lawful step-outs rather than disengagement, which is itself worth knowing before assuming a raw absence rate reflects how often councillors simply don't show up.

question_technical: What share of decided items is confidential, and is it rising?
title_technical: How much business is taken behind closed doors?
objection: A spike in confidential business coinciding with a period of active external scrutiny looks like the opposite of transparency — hiding more precisely when outsiders were watching closest.
response: The long-run baseline is a genuinely open record, and a period of active external scrutiny legitimately generates confidential business — legal advice and personnel matters under active investigation — so some rise in those years is expected, and it reverted once scrutiny ended. That concedes the pattern is not baseline behaviour. What it still raises is the *scale* of the spike and its *timing* relative to the scrutiny period: read in the round, this reads as a transparent council that went unusually quiet during a period of active scrutiny, not a habitually secretive one.

question_technical: Do confidential tenders carry higher dollar values than open ones?
title_technical: Are the redacted tenders the bigger contracts?
objection: The confidential-tender sample here is small, and most confidential tenders don't even record a dollar figure at all — a pattern built on so few priced observations could easily be noise, not a real difference in contract size.
response: The small sample is why this is stated as directional rather than definitive. But the gap this measure can't see cuts the other way: tenders missing a recorded amount are excluded from the comparison entirely, and that missingness biases toward understating any real difference, not manufacturing one — so a small but real sample is, if anything, an undersell of the true gap. Confidentiality on a tender is often lawful in its own right, so this is a visibility concern rather than evidence of impropriety.

question_technical: Does confidentiality track lawful statutory grounds or politically contentious topics?
title_technical: What subject matter gets closed — and is it the contentious stuff?
objection: Keyword bucketing of item descriptions is a noisy way to classify what confidentiality is protecting — a genuinely contentious item described in bland administrative language could be miscounted as routine, understating how much sensitive material gets closed.
response: That noise is acknowledged directly and it biases in the safer direction: coarse keyword matching is more likely to over-count development-related closures than to hide them, so a result showing the most contentious topic is the *least* closed is, if anything, a conservative reading in the council's favour, not a generous one.

question_technical: Do tender dollars cluster into the final months of the budget cycle?
title_technical: Is there an end-of-year 'use it or lose it' spike?
objection: Comparing one month's dollar share against a flat even-spread baseline assumes spending should land evenly across the year — but capital works and infrastructure contracts are naturally lumpy, so some concentration in any one month doesn't by itself indicate budget-cycle gaming.
response: The test is built with that in mind: it isn't asking whether the final month differs from the baseline at all, but whether it differs by enough to look like a deliberate use-it-or-lose-it dump rather than ordinary lumpy capital timing — and the threshold for calling that a concern is set well above the even-spread expectation, not at it.

question_technical: Are reserves being depleted (the s.114 precursor)?
title_technical: Reserve depletion / financial resilience
objection: Without the data this corpus would need to compute it, there is no way to see whether reserves are being run down over time — a real gap in financial-resilience oversight, not a clean result.
response: As with the other not-computable tests in this battery, carrying the gap here rather than dropping the test keeps it visible and comparable: a council whose minutes do carry reserve-balance figures will produce a real answer, and this blank result is a flagged re-extraction target, not a silent pass.

question_technical: What is the volume and trend of public questions, deputations and petitions?
title_technical: How much does the public take part?
objection: Counting how many public questions, deputations and petitions were recorded says nothing about whether the council actually listened or changed course in response — a high count could just as easily mean a council that hears a lot and ignores all of it.
response: This test is deliberately a volume measure, not an influence measure — participation actually mattering is what the responsiveness and dose-response tests elsewhere in this battery are for. Knowing how much the public shows up at all is still the necessary first fact before asking whether it changes anything.

question_technical: Do meetings with a public deputation see more contested votes?
title_technical: Do public deputations make for stormier meetings?
objection: A meeting having a deputation and a meeting having more contested motions could both simply be symptoms of a busy, high-stakes agenda — the correlation alone can't tell whether deputations make meetings livelier or just tend to land on nights that were already going to be contested.
response: That confound is stated plainly rather than papered over: the small gap found here is read as inconclusive precisely because busy meetings independently attract both more deputations and more contested motions, not as evidence either way about deputations' own effect.

question_technical: What share of public questions are deferred rather than answered in the meeting, over time?
title_technical: Are residents' questions answered, or quietly 'taken on notice'?
objection: Most public questions are still answered in the meeting — the great majority get a live answer, so this isn't really a responsiveness problem.
response: What matters is the shift, not the level: deferral rose substantially once the council came under a period of heightened external scrutiny and never fully returned to its earlier baseline — and the measure, if anything, understates that shift. Part of the single-year peak is a remote-meeting artefact (meetings went online and complex questions were reasonably answered in writing), but the rise began before the remote period and persisted well after it ended, so a temporary shift to remote meetings doesn't carry the trend on its own. 'Taken on notice' is lawful and often appropriate for complex questions, so this reads as a responsiveness concern, not impropriety.
